speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: We had conducted engagement sessions with selected societies in 2022 and 2023, as well as a public consultation exercise in 2022 via the REACH platform.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The feedback was supportive of the proposed amendments.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: First, we aim to strengthen the registration process.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Currently, applications to register societies can be processed via two routes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The Normal Route is for applications that fall within the categories specified in the Schedule of the Societies Act.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: These societies are involved in issues which are more sensitive, such as politics, religion, race, language and nationality.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Such applications go through vetting and assessment by the Registrar of Societies, which may involve several rounds of clarifications with the applicant.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The Registrar has the authority to reject applications submitted via the Normal Route.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This was introduced in 2004, for applications that do not fall within the categories specified in the Schedule of the Societies Act.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: It is meant for societies involved in issues which are less sensitive.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: For these applications, the Societies Act currently states that the Registrar shall, without making any further inquiry, register these societies on the date the Registrar receives the application, so long as the formal requirements for registration are met.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: In the last five years, we received about 1,400 applications.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: About half of them were submitted via the Automatic Route.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This differentiated approach in processing applications has allowed MHA to focus its attention on assessing the more sensitive applications.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: First, there were instances when the Registrar needed information to ascertain whether applications under the Automatic Route indeed did not fall within the sensitive categories in the Schedule of the Societies Act.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: However, the current law does not allow the Registrar to seek clarifications of such applications.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Second, even if an application does not fall within the sensitive categories in the Schedule, it could still be of concern.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: However, the Registrar currently has no authority to reject such applications.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Suppose a group of individuals, with antecedents of concern, wished to set up a society to advocate for the interest of a racial group.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: However, they know that if they were to set up a society promoting the interests of a particular race, they would have to do so via the Normal Route, where the Registrar would be able to scrutinise their application, such as asking questions to clarify the objectives of the society and queries on their leadership composition.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: To avoid being questioned, this group tries to set up a society with an innocuous aim, such as a history interest group.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Such an application could then be submitted via the Automatic Route, which currently, will be approved immediately.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The proposed amendments in the Bill would allow the Registrar to make inquiries on all applications submitted, for both Automatic and Normal Routes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Clause 4 of the Bill adds a new section to allow appeals to the Minister for Home Affairs for rejected applications via the Automatic Route, similar to the existing appeal mechanism for applications via the Normal Route.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: If an appeal is rejected by the Minister, the applicants can launch a judicial review, no different from today.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: We expect the majority of applications for registration of societies to still go through the Automatic Route without the need for any clarifications.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Our next set of amendments seeks to clarify the Registrar’s powers for applications submitted via the Normal Route.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Currently, under the Normal Route, the Registrar may request an applicant to insert clauses into their constitution, prior to allowing the registration of the society.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This practice is in accordance with section 29(1)(b) of the Interpretation Act, which provides that a power to grant a licence, permit, approval or exemption, also includes the power to impose reasonable conditions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: For instance, to preserve Singapore’s multi-religious and multiracial harmony, the Registrar may request an applicant of a society that is involved in issues of race and religion to insert a clause that the society "shall not engage in any activities that may undermine racial or religious harmony in Singapore", as a condition for registration.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Clause 3 of the Bill inserts a new section 4(3A) to make it explicit that the Registrar has powers to require the rules of specified societies to be amended as a condition for registration.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The Registrar can refuse to register the society if the society does not comply.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Section 4(3A) does not list the grounds for which the Registrar will direct a specified society to amend its rules.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: However, this does not mean that the Registrar can require a society to include unreasonable rules into its Constitution, failing which the Registrar will reject an application.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The Registrar’s decisions must still have a nexus to the purpose of the Societies Act, which is to ensure that groups which may be used for unlawful purposes, or poses a threat to public order, welfare or good order in Singapore or which will be contrary to our national interests will not be established in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Currently, under section 11 of the Societies Act, societies need to seek the Registrar’s approval to change their name or amend the rules in their constitution.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The Societies Act is silent on the grounds on which the Registrar can refuse to approve such applications.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: For example, the Registrar can refuse to approve a change in name if the new name is likely to mislead members of the public as to the true character or purpose of the society.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The Registrar can refuse to approve a change in the constitution if it would be contrary to Singapore’s national interest or prejudicial to public peace, welfare or good order in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: For avoidance of doubt, the Registrar will not be limited to the grounds stated in the Act.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Under section 12(1)(b) of the Societies Act, the Minister can currently declare a person to be unfit to be an officer of a society by reason of any conviction for a criminal offence, for example, where the officer is convicted for dishonesty, such as fraud, scam, cheating or misuse of monies, as well as offences under the Societies Act.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: An "officer" here refers to committee members and does not include members of the society.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: A person who is declared to be unfit by the Registrar can apply to the Minister for permission to act as an officer of a society.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Currently, section 2 of the Societies Act defines the place of business of a registered society as "the place where the records and books of account of a society is kept".

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This is too narrow in today’s context where virtual offices and storage of documents on the cloud are common.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Instead of place of business, clause 2 of the Bill amends section 2 of the Societies Act to refer to "registered address" instead, defined as the address of the society that is kept and maintained with the Registrar.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Consequential amendments will be made throughout the Societies Act.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The next set of amendments are on the offences.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: In addition, we have updated the offences of providing false information to the Registrar.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Currently, sections 10 and 29 of the Societies Act penalise the failure to provide information and the provision of false information to the Registrar.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Clauses 7 and 14 of the Bill update these provisions to align with the language used in newer Acts, such as the Debt Collection Act.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: In particular, on the provision of false information to the Registrar, the fault element of the offender is presently not mentioned in sections 10 and 29.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This means that even if a person provided false or inaccurate information by mistake, he would be in breach.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: MHA's view is that only those who intentionally, knowingly or recklessly provide false or inaccurate information should be liable.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Clauses 7 and 14 of the Bill, therefore, amend the fault element of these offences accordingly.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Clause 15 of the Bill introduces a new section 30A to allow the Registrar to compound offences in the Societies Act as an alternative to charging offenders in Court.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The Bill also includes amendments to facilitate the administration and regulation of societies.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: First, we are proposing amendments to allow for electronic transmission of documents.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: These are in clauses 5, 6, 7, 9, 11 and 16 of the Bill.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Second, currently, application fees are to be paid upon approval of applications before the society is registered.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: MHA intends to charge the fee upon submission of an application, as costs will have to be incurred to assess the application, regardless of whether the registration is approved.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Clauses 3 and 4 of the Bill give effect to this.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Third, societies which are charities presently have to file their annual submissions to two separate authorities, the Registry of Societies and Charities Unit.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Clause 17 of the Bill introduces new sections to allow the Registrar to prescribe different forms for them.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Under Article 14(1)(c) of the Constitution, all citizens of Singapore have the right to form associations.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Article 14(2) specifically provides that Parliament may impose restrictions by law as it considers necessary or expedient in the interest of the security of Singapore, public order or morality.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Further, Article 14(3) allows Parliament to impose, by law, restrictions relating to labour or education.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Societies Act 1966 is a piece of legislation that Parliament passed to impose the restrictions contemplated in Article 14(2).

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We can appreciate, therefore, that the Act performs an important gatekeeping function.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: These include situations where, in the opinion of the Registrar, the specified society is likely to be used for unlawful purposes or for purposes prejudicial to public peace as contemplated in Article 14(2) of the Constitution.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Save for the enumerated circumstances, it is provided in section 4(1) of the Act that the Registrar shall register the society upon certain conditions being fulfilled.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The current arrangement makes good sense as it gives primacy to the constitutional right of Singaporeans to form associations, save in certain circumstances.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: At the same time, there is clarity on the basis upon which the Registrar can reject a society’s application.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This was specifically acknowledged by Assoc Prof Ho Peng Kee in this House in the same speech.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He said and I quote, "In the first instance, the Registrar will have the discretion to look at applications.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But his discretion is not an unfettered one… He bases his discretion on the Act itself.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: On the face of it, it is proposed that the Registrar is to be given a certain measure of discretion to decide whether or not to register a specified society.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: On the face of it, the ambit of discretion is not specifically spelt out, save that it is subject to several circumstances set out in section 4 where the Registrar has the specific power to refuse registration of specified societies.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In a similar vein, I seek the hon Minister of State's explanation on the proposal to vest in the Registrar the power to not register a specified society unless the rules of the society include or exclude provisions that the Registrar may direct.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is set out in clause 3(c) of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Again, having regard to the constitutional provisions that I have highlighted earlier in my speech, may I ask what the ambit of this power will be?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And I understand from the hon Minister of State's speech that it is meant to be used where national interests are engaged.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But interestingly, unlike the power when you are dealing with amendments of rules, which is spelt out in clause 8(c) of the Bill, the grounds in respect of which the Registrar may invoke a direction to amend the rules is absent, when it comes to requiring the applicant to amend the rules at the point of application before the society is even registered.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So, there is a dichotomy in the approach.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: That was, in turn, derived from a recommendation by the Remaking Singapore Committee, chaired by then Minister of State for National Development, Dr Vivian Balakrishnan, to adopt a differentiated approach by listing down explicitly the types of societies that would require prior approval.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Those outside the list would be "automatically" approved and registered.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Committee added a caveat that the registrations of such societies could still be revoked if they were subsequently found to use the society for unlawful purposes.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: MHA then consulted the public on this and public feedback was generally supportive.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: MHA then finetuned the feedback received and finalised the scheme.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: During the Second Reading of the Bill in 2004, the then Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs, Assoc Prof Ho Peng Kee, said that the amendments would "make it easier for many societies to be registered" and that "the changes are in line with the Government's move to loosen up restrictions to encourage greater social entrepreneurship." He called this automatic regime a "forward-looking approach".

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It seeks to allow the Registrar to require further information to ascertain whether the society does, indeed, qualify for registration via the Automatic Route.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Thus, if the 2004 amendments were a "forward-looking approach", this Bill appears to be a backward-looking approach.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Why are the amendments to the automatic registration route now necessary?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: What has changed between 2004, when they were introduced, and now?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Section 24(1) of the Act already empowers the Minister to dissolve a society if it had secured automatic registration through false declaration or misrepresentation of its objects and activities at the point of registration.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: If there is need for an addition to the list of specified societies listed in the Schedule, the Minister is already empowered under section 33A to amend the Schedule by notification in the Gazette.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: If the society engages in illegal activities, it can be dealt with through a whole host of laws to safeguard national security and racial and religious harmony.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Minister of State has cited hypothetical examples.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Does she have real examples of society applications submitted since 2004 under the Automatic Route where one or both of the "two gaps" she mentioned were breached?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: What instances were there of registrations of non-specified societies that posed a national security threat and should not have been registered and how did the Registrar deal with those cases?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: How many applications to form societies were rejected or refused registration by the Registrar in the past five years and what were the reasons for their rejection or refusal of registration?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Since 2004, we have seen a proliferation of access to the worldwide web, social media, smartphones and artificial intelligence.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: There is no shortage of data for the authorities to conduct background checks on applicants, even without asking them for more information.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Additionally, questionnaires can be built into the online application form and the applicants' answers to these questions could be used to flag out societies that are not eligible for the automatic registration route.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The applicant can then be immediately notified to select the normal registration route before submitting their application.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: If all these gates fail and the society gets registered through misrepresentation, the Minister can dissolve the society under section 24(1).

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Groups nowadays can easily organise themselves over closed chatgroups and will likely avoid going through the hassle of registering a society if it is made more onerous.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It will impose a greater burden on law-abiding groups who diligently register their societies.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: By placing more hurdles for groups seeking to organise formally, the unintended effect could be to drive them and their activities underground.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: When this happens, the Registry of Societies will lose regulatory oversight of their financial conduct, which is one area where regulation is necessary in the public interest.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Can the Minister of State assure the House that genuine applications under the Automatic Route will not face longer waiting periods for approval than under the current regime?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The inclusion of these types of societies in the Schedule means that they cannot be registered under the Automatic Route.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Assoc Prof Ho Peng Kee said in 2004 that "such groups, which aim to promote a particular cause, can potentially give rise to law and order problems if they engage actively in pushing their agenda, without due regard for those who may not agree with their cause." Is this still the Government's position and, more importantly, is that the only reason?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I look forward to the Minister of State's answers to my questions.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 4.05 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 3.45 pm until 4.05 pm.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They serve as platforms for the development of strong bonds and community relations, uniting individuals from various social and cultural backgrounds.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: By forming a society, these groups establish a common identity among members who share a specific objective or purpose.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Societies provide a setting for members to engage in discussions or activities related to particular interests or issues in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I appreciate MHA's effort in simplifying the process for registration of societies in the past.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, despite existing regulations governing the registration of societies, the evolving societal dynamics and complex international environment have made it more challenging to manage the risks and threats associated with social groups.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is essential to strike a balance between enabling the formation of societies and ensuring that these groups do not pose risks to national security or public order.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe that the proposed amendment aims to serve this very purpose.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, I seek to understand the methodology that the Registrar will employ to make these judgements.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How comprehensive will the vetting process be and what measures will be put in place to ensure that societies with potential risks are effectively identified?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Additionally, I would like to clarify with MHA on the specific criteria that will be employed to assess whether societies are engaged in unlawful activities that will be prejudicial to public peace, welfare or good order in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This will offer greater clarity to the public, as well as existing and prospective societies, on the conditions that must be met to ensure compliance.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This provides a means for groups to be able to seek redress if they feel that they have a strong case for registration.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This appeal process ensures opportunity for due process and serves as an important check-and-balance mechanism.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Lastly, it is worth noting the susceptibility of registered societies in Singapore to foreign influence interests through covert operations.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We are reminded that in today's globalised world, the reach of foreign powers is not limited by borders and this makes the regulations of our societies even more imperative.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope to understand how MHA intends to combat that in this amendment Bill.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While clause 9 of the amendment Bill, which modifies section 11A, clearly empowers the Registrar to mandate rule changes for specified societies as a condition for registration, I am concerned if this is sufficient to manage potential risks.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This formal compliance might appease the authorities on paper, but there remains the risk that the society in question could continue to pursue unlawful objectives.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Therefore, I seek clarification from MHA on the mechanisms in place to ensure that undue foreign influence does not infiltrate specified societies discussing or promoting issues related to sensitive issues.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Additionally, will non-specified societies be directed or asked to modify their constitutions if they are identified as engaging in causes that seem to discuss or promote issues that are not aligned with a specific policy or the national interest of Singapore?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In closing, Mr Deputy Speaker, we cannot overlook the delicate balance that must be maintained between allowing societies and interest groups to grow and safeguarding national security.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Internal security is of paramount importance to safeguard Singapore against social divisions that destabilise and tear apart any social fabric.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As I have raised earlier, we must ensure that our legal frameworks are robust enough to protect our community groups from being exploited for unlawful purposes.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As such, the registration of our societies, whether specified under the Schedule of the Societies Act or not, should advance objectives in promoting communal harmony and the interest of all Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: More relevant and presently, I am the President of Lembaga Biasiswa Kenangan Maulud and Honorary Secretary of Singapore Psychiatric Association.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: And I also have memberships in a few other registered societies.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: It also suggests and reinforces that we make no apologies in protecting our Singapore society against undesirable and offensive influences that could fracture us along naturally occurring differences, such as religious and racial identities, or against ideas that are rooted in illegal activities or arising from foreign interference.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: I am also heartened that the Bill's reach goes wide enough to be able to hold accountable persons who, directly or by proxy, allow any unlawful assembly, induce membership, publish materials and procure subscription and aid for the purposes of such unlawful societies.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: I think these rules are necessary and the spirit of the amendments keeps pace with our desire to protect society against such detrimental activities.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: These can range from issues relating to ethnicity, to religion, to nationality or language, to political inclinations, to civil liberties and rights, to the environment and even to animal welfare.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, the importance of societies within our society cannot be understated.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: Societies are like ingredients to the recipe of what Singapore is and could become.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: And beyond political affiliations in this House, I can say with a degree of confidence that many hon Members of the House are, or previously have been, members of societies and ground-up initiatives as well.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: The nature of the establishment of any one society necessarily involves a group of people invested in a particular topic or issue enough to want to make formal a cause to call their collective own.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: It tells of a tale of a determined advocacy and of a meeting of intellectual minds and of a sense of belonging via a common thread, theme and identity.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: By extension, this adds much richness and diversity to Singapore because societies, directly or indirectly, develop a rootedness to the local community, allow for outlets of philanthropy and groom the next generation of community leadership.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: The thing about new ideas though, especially those without precedent and appearing as foreign and unfamiliar at the onset, is that they may well be seen as an affront initially to the current norm and equilibrium.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: New ideas could be viewed with much doubt, cynicism or even distrust by the establishment.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: I hope that while the Ministry maintains its firm hand on the powers accorded by the Bill to be decisive when it comes to issues of national interest and security, that it also tempers the weight of this responsibility with an even-handed approach to some novelty, creativity, youthful exuberance and unusual ideas so that Singapore society can flourish from the diversity in our societies.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: Beyond looking at the current laws and regulations, one must also recognise that the texture and grain of societies registered in any one era of our history tell us, to some extent, the matters of interest, influence and advocacy of the larger Singapore society then.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: Even as the Ministry is able to exercise its powers and authority, I would urge that the Ministry consider with some nuance, discernment and concern any dissolution of societies that have a long history, track record and legacy alongside Singapore's history.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: It may well be that the cause remains as true, important and relevant today as it did pre-Independence, and it is just that the current prevailing interest, strength in leadership or continuity remain a temporary but periodic challenge for that particular society.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: Rather than reinventing new organisations at every turn, I urge some discretion to give time and support for such societies, steeped in history and legacy, to recalibrate its identity and reinvigorate itself anew rather than be dissolved.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: (In Malay): The Societies (Amendment) Bill encompasses, among others, Malay/Muslim community organisations which have existed for a long time and did a lot of good for the community since the 1960s.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: Apart from LBKM, there are also other organisations like Alwehdah, Jamiyah, PERDAUS, PPIS and 4PM which have served for decades in community matters.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: These organisations have their own emphasis and focus based on their areas of expertise and specialisation.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: Although their specific focus area may be different, just like the interdependent bamboo and riverbank, these organisations have shown a desire to work together to address the concerns of the community and the nation.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: These organisations have a strong link to Singapore's history and have sculpted, shaped and influenced the lives of our community in Singapore together.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: It is normal that many youths want to try out new interests and, sometimes, these interests seem to go against the cultural norms of the day.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: Although the sculpture may appear different, the style, nonetheless, remains the same: these youths have a deep desire and commitment to serve and uplift society.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time, I also call on youths and professionals to contribute to prominent organisations, and it is not something that is old-fashioned or backward; far from it.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, lately, the torch of leadership in some organisations have already been passed on to the next generation of leaders.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: They still value legacy and history and have gained confidence and benefited from the knowledge and experience of past leaders.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: New and contemporary ideas may sometimes cause misunderstanding initially due to differences in perspective, but if these ideas essentially stem from a desire to uplift society together, I think we should allow such ideas to be explored.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: Sooner or later, changes and new ideas will become inevitable.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, a sign of a maturing society is when it gives due attention to renewal and recalibration after careful consideration.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: I am also of the view that civil society needs space to flourish and grow as well, because the nature of interests, texture of advocacy and the tenor of the times will certainly shift as the years go by.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: And as these shift, tension will surely exist now and then between new, seemingly disruptive ideas and the prevailing social norm.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: These may be seen as presenting a challenge to the existing good order of things initially.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: The proposed changes will enable societies to function effectively while remaining vigilant to the vulnerabilities and threats that may affect the society, its members and beneficiaries.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: These regulatory measures are necessary to ensure public safety and security.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: It is important to note that the need for regulation and oversight of registered societies goes beyond enforcing laws and norms.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: They act as preventive measures, deterring potential wrongdoers from engaging in harmful activities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: By providing clear guidelines and enforcing consequences, regulations create a culture of accountability, discouraging individuals from taking advantage of others or exploiting loopholes for personal gain.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Societies complement the Government's service delivery, foster civic engagement and play a crucial role in addressing social and economic issues, such as poverty, healthcare, housing and education.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Their programmes and services can assist, improve the quality of life for vulnerable populations, reduce inequality and discrimination and promote social inclusion.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: We need to recognise and celebrate their contribution.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: It is, however, also important to remember the increasing threats connected with societies and it is reasonable that the Government provide some level of regulation and oversight of societies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: This regulation and oversight must, however, be proportionate to the need.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: The provision of clear and informative reasons will assist societies to better understand and comply with required rules and regulations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: The provision of separate registration routes reflects a risk-based approach.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: It assures societies ease of registration and also allows societies the option of opting for automatic registration based on their mandate and objectives.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Considering that some societies may be of higher risk and some may represent little or no risk at all, the proposed changes will strengthen the Registrar's capacity to examine the registration of societies that may pose harm to public safety.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Apart from making further enquiry or requiring new societies to include specific rules in their constitution, may I suggest that selected societies be required to include a detailed description of their governing body or management committee and the stipulated duties of its members at the point of registration and for this information to be evaluated and audited.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: An example of a similar requirement can be found in the New Zealand Incorporated Societies Act 2022.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: That Act defines six specific duties for officers, including to act in good faith and in the best interests of the society and exercise reasonable care and diligence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: This was explained yesterday at the Ministerial Statement on Singapore's Anti-money Laundering Regime.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: However, considering the complexity of fulfilling required financial obligations, may I suggest that those societies classified to be at higher risk of exploitation by bad actors be given additional support and guidance?

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: This would also allow members to consider novel financial regulations, such as the use of smart contracts on blockchain platforms to automatically release funds or utilising blockchain technology to maintain an immutable ledger of financial transactions and activities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Apart from financial issues, I am concerned about young people and vulnerable individuals joining a society and being groomed into engaging in undesirable or criminal activities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: There is also the danger of members being victimised.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: This is a real threat, considering the proliferation of fake news, the ease of connectivity online and potentially negative influence arising from online gatherings.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: A society can be formed with all good intent, yet, over time, have their meetings infiltrated or influenced by new, sometimes anonymous, members and end up discussing or promoting dangerous or extreme topics of ideologies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Another area of concern is related to technology and the formation of online groups on various digital platforms.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: It is harder to monitor and establish the underlying intention of such groups.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: In view of the potential threats and challenges, would the Ministry consider providing online or other options to allow societies to ask questions and seek guidance and support about their compliance obligations?

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: To promote responsible engagement and giving, it is important to share information with the public.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Would the Ministry consider developing public awareness campaigns to educate volunteers and the public about the importance of supporting ethical and compliant society?

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: I am pleased to note that members of the public can search the database for registered societies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: However, to access further details about the society, they need to purchase that information.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This Act, in its previous iterations and at present, ensures that groups with the potential for unlawful activities, threats to national security or activities contrary to our nation's interests, do not gain traction or growth within our borders.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Notwithstanding, I have several clarifications on the Bill.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Furthermore, if the members of the would-be society find itself in disagreement with the clauses prescribed by the Registrar, what recourse do they have against the Registrar's decision?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Likewise, in the event of a registration being denied, what avenues exist for societies to appeal such decisions?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Second, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, as we delve into the provision detailing the grounds that the Registrar can consider when evaluating applications for amendments in rules and names, as well as addressing concerns regarding foreign interference, several queries come to mind.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will the Bill provide a comprehensive list of considerations for societies to reference?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Could there potentially be a reference guide or illustrative examples, akin to a "blacklist," to assist applicants in navigating this process with clarity?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Would this entail the application of the Foreign Interference Countermeasures Act, or FICA, concerning the registration of such societies?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In addition, how will this Bill regulate societies with foreign affiliations, particularly those with undisclosed intentions?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will societies be mandated to declare such affiliations before they are allowed to be registered?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This heightened scrutiny is warranted to prevent potential cases of money laundering and tax evasion.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Third, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, as we turn our attention to groups that are organised in virtual spaces, within chat groups and on the Internet, a set of unique challenges arises.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Earlier, Member Assoc Prof Razwana Begum mentioned this as well.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Are there plans to expressly address these societies under the Act?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If so, what conditions will be set forth for their registration?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Particularly, when these societies operate on a secure or private platforms provided by companies that are not governed by Singapore's laws, ensuring compliance in the digital realm becomes a complex undertaking.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is important to address how the respective agencies plan to police this expansive digital landscape, given the evolving nature of technology.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Laws, no matter how well-crafted, are only effective if they can be enforced.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: On this note, I would also like to inquire about the nature and extent of cooperation that Singapore has established or intends to establish with companies that provide digital services and products that allow online societies to form, specifically regarding the objectives of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Examples may be Telegram, Facebook groups and WhatsApp.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Cooperation on a global scale is imperative to effectively address the challenges posed by societies operating in the digital sphere.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will the Ministry establish an entirely new portal for this purpose or will it be seamlessly integrated with the existing MHA iROSES system?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Today, there are entities, such as religious organisations, that have the option to register both as societies and as charities.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Is there an intention to streamline this process?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Additionally, how do we educate the public about the appropriate steps to take in such cases?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Last but not least, it is essential to recognise that the workload on the Registrar of Societies, or ROS, will inevitably increase.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This raises important questions about whether ROS will need to recalibrate its processes, potentially requiring additional manpower.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How will ROS collaborate with the Police to share the workload and ensure seamless distribution of information?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As we reflect upon its implications in the present day, we are compelled to redefine our perspective on the types of societies that necessitate regulation in today's landscape, with the paramount goal of safeguarding our national security.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In this digital age, we must re-evaluate our approach to society regulation, acknowledging that many of these entities operate predominantly in virtual spaces, transcending national boundaries in an era of globalisation and digitalisation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Some may not readily disclose their true agendas, underscoring the need for a regulatory framework that empowers the Government to act swiftly and effectively when necessary.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This involves not only implementing the necessary regulations, but also having the resources to monitor, as well as the levers to enforce the rules.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Only through this holistic approach can we adequately address the challenges posed by societies in today's dynamic and interconnected world.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Registry of Societies' website says that the earliest piece of legislation relating to societies was the Dangerous Societies Suppression Ordinance in 1869.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It had the aim of eliminating secret societies in the Straits Settlement.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But since then, the types of societies we see has expanded, as small ground-up initiatives and small groups come together and formalise – a society being seen as a simpler and more straightforward framework of governance and reporting, than say a private limited entity.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many form a dynamic part of our social fabric.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have three brief points on the Bill.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It will appear to some that, given the amendments, perhaps we should have just one route that is non-automatic and the Registrar can ask the relevant questions if necessary.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I would thus like to ask the Minister of State about the scope and interpretation of "purposes prejudicial to public peace, welfare or good order" and any key principles of those which are likely to be rejected and hope that this can be outlined for greater clarity.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Failure to do so can impede an application.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Section 11A of the Societies Act outlines the grounds on which the Registrar considers for an application to change the rules – I understand that this would be similar to my previous point – would be contrary to Singapore's national interests or security, would be prejudicial to public peace, welfare, good order or contrary to the Act.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, these are fairly broad and it would be helpful if the Minister of State could provide greater clarity on the criteria.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How far will the Government intervene in recommending the language or the rules to be included?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am also heartened to note the amendments which cater for the electronic transmission of service documents.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Such amendments relate to enhancing convenience and bring greater accessibility.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Organisations, such as the Singapore Cancer Society, Silver Ribbon Singapore and Cornerstone Community Services, are societies with charitable and social purposes that do a lot for our community here in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is important for societies to be governed well by their office-bearers.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Are there any opportunities for office-bearers to receive governance training or any minimum age and experience required to be an office-bearer of a society?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: On a small note, I also note that individuals with prior convictions may not be permitted to hold office in societies.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Given our push in advocating for second chances – and many of us have seen the hard work and determination of ex-offenders who have turned over a new leaf and want to support others in turn, for example, as a desistor – what possibilities are there and channels for such individuals to become leaders of such groups, for a fair assessment of their suitability?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To conclude, Sir, many such organisations first start off as an informal smaller ground-up initiative and later put forth an application under this Act, because a form of formal recognition as a legal entity is helpful before they can access grants and funding for their organisation to be sustainable in the long term.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Choosing to register as a legal entity, in this case, as a society, is no easy step as many of the members are volunteers with full-time jobs.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is crucial to ensure that the process is simple, efficient and friendly to encourage a thriving people-sector, where like-minded people passionate about causes, such as the environment, mental health and youth empowerment, can exchange ideas, advocate for their concerns and take action.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope more can be done on a wider level to support groups, such as these, who choose to take the step of registration, including potentially considering a new type of legal entity, for such cause-based ground-up initiatives.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Notwithstanding the above, Mr Speaker, Sir, I support the Bill.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Ms Ng Ling Ling asked how the Registrar of Societies would assess whether an application, submitted via the Automatic Route, would pose risks to national security or public order, or be prejudicial to public peace, welfare or good order in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: This assessment looks at many factors, such as the background of the applicants, the proposed activities of the society and the nature of their foreign affiliations.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Ms Ng asked whether non-specified societies will be directed to modify their constitutions if they are identified as engaging in causes that seem to discuss or promote issues aligned with a specific policy objective.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The answer is yes, and the current law already allows us to do it.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Ms Ng and Mr Yip spoke about the appeals for societies whose applications are rejected.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Questions on how many appeals have been reviewed over the years by the Minister for specified and non-specified societies and on what grounds the appeals are granted by the Minister were asked.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Currently, non-specified societies are automatically registered and cannot be rejected.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: All appeals received by the Minister are for specified societies rejected through the Normal Route.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: In assessing statutory appeals, the Minister will have to weigh the views of the applicants against the Registrar's.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The grounds of acceding to or rejecting the appeal are fact-specific.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Gerald Giam asked why we need to amend the Automatic Route.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: MHA reviews its laws and regulations regularly to ensure that they remain up-to-date.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: These amendments are part of our regular review.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: I can also assure this House that genuine applications under the Automatic Route will not face a longer waiting period for approvals than under the current regime.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: For operational reasons, we seek Members’ understanding that we are not able to share more about these three applications and, for their own reasons which we do not know, the applicants did not pursue their applications.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Giam also asked, instead of amending the Automatic Route, why not expand the Schedule to include more categories?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: We will still need to allow the Registrar to ask questions as we need to be able to assess whether the application does, indeed, fall outside the categories in the Schedule.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Sometimes, the Registrar may not be able to assess based purely on the details submitted in the application.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Giam suggested that questionnaires be built into the application form to help identify societies whether they should be submitted via the Normal or Automatic Route.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Applicants have to answer a set of questions as part of the application process.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Based on their replies, the system will route to either the Automatic or the Normal Route.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: However, as mentioned, there could be instances where the Registrar may need to make enquiries to ascertain whether the declarations were done correctly, for example, when the objectives in their draft constitution indicate a function covered in the Schedule, but yet their declaration indicated otherwise.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: In such a situation, the amendments would allow the Registrar to ask questions.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Giam asked for examples of applications that were submitted via the Automatic Route but should have been submitted via the Normal Route.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Applicants make incorrect declarations, though without ill-intent, that result in their applications sent via the wrong route.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Currently, pugilistic or martial arts fall within the categories in the Schedule.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Hence, applications for societies that deal with pugilistic or martial arts have to be submitted via the Normal Route.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: An applicant clicked "no" on the question pertaining to whether it is a martial arts group, thinking that it is a sports group.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: However, ROS reviewed the application and found that its constitution listed martial arts as an activity.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: ROS then moved it to the Normal Route instead.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Murali Pillai highlighted the change from "shall" to "may" in section 4(1) of the Societies Act.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Currently, section 4 of the Societies Act provides that the Registrar shall register a specified society upon application and payment of the prescribed fee unless one of the grounds for refusal in section 4 applies.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Currently, the prescribed fee is paid only upon approval of application.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Hence, upon payment of the fees, the Registrar must – shall – register the society.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: We are amending the Societies Act to state that the prescribed fee is be paid upon application, instead of upon approval.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: This means that, after the payment of fees, the Registrar might still refuse to register the society based on one of the grounds in section 4.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Therefore, it is inaccurate to mandate that the Registrar must register the society upon payment of the prescribed fee.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: To be clear, if none of the grounds for refusal in section 4 is made out, the Registrar will not refuse to register the society.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Hence, the amendment remains aligned with Article 14 of the Constitution and the purpose of section 4, as stated by then Senior Minister of State Assoc Prof Ho Peng Kee in 2004.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Murali also asked about the ambit of the Registrar’s powers to mandate the inclusion or exclusion of provisions of the constitution of a specified society before registration.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: He further asked how this power will be exercised in conformity with Article 14 of the Constitution.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: To clarify, as mentioned in my opening speech, this is not a new power.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: This practice is in accordance with section 29(1)(b) of the Interpretation Act, which provides that a power to grant approval also includes the power to impose reasonable conditions.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The amendment to the Societies Act simply makes this power explicit.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The Registrar’s discretion is not unfettered; his decisions must still have a nexus to Singapore’s security, public order or morality.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Hence, even with the amendments, the Registrar’s powers must still be exercised in line with Article 14 of the Constitution.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: To answer Mr Yip Hong Weng’s question on the recourse if there are disagreements on the rules being inserted, applicants can write to the Registry of Societies and we will consider each case on a case-by-case basis.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Giam asked why societies discussing issues related to civil or political rights or the governance of Singapore society remain listed in the Schedule.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: These are sensitive issues and need to be appropriately handled by the society in order for it not to become a socially divisive one.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: In some cases, they could also be a channel for foreign influence into sensitive domestic affairs.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Hence, societies that cover these areas should apply via the Normal Route.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Yip asked for clarity on the list of considerations for amendments of rule and name.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: This is provided for in the amendments under clause 8 of the Bill, which listed the grounds of which the application to change name and rules will be rejected.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Societies can also refer to the "Frequently Asked Questions" on the Registry of Societies' website for guidelines on amendments of rules and names.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum noted that the Bill would provide clarity on the reasons why applications to change names and rules are rejected.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: I wish to clarify that the amendments in clause 8 of the Bill list the grounds on which the Registrar can reject applications to change names or rules.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: It does not legally require the Registrar to provide reasons for rejecting the applications to change names or rules.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Having said that, ROS will engage the applicants and advise, where appropriate, as long as it does not involve the disclosure of sensitive information.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: We had several questions on the grounds of rejection.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Giam asked how many applications to form societies were rejected in the past five years and what were the grounds for their rejection.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: On the grounds of rejecting an application for registration, Ms Nadia Samdin asked when the Registrar would consider an application to be prejudicial to public peace, welfare or good order.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Ms Nadia also asked when the Registrar would refuse an application to amend the rules of a society on the grounds that it is contrary to national interests or security, prejudicial to public peace, welfare or good order, or contrary to the Societies Act.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Murali also asked questions in a similar vein on how the powers based on these grounds would be exercised.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The grounds for rejection for those via the Normal Route are as stated in sections 4(2) and 4(3) of the Societies Act.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: For example, an application may be rejected if the society was likely to be used for unlawful purposes, or for purposes prejudicial to public peace, welfare or good order in Singapore, or that it would be contrary to national security or interest for the society to be registered.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The Registrar considers many factors in assessing whether an application should be rejected based on the grounds in the Societies Act and in the Bill.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Applications for registration may be refused where doing so is necessary to: prevent social segregation or religious and racial disharmony; safeguard Singapore against foreign interference; or protect public safety or Singapore’s security in general.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Applications to amend rules may be rejected if the rules would lead to a breach of the Societies Act or the Societies Regulations.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: For example, section 12 of the Societies Act prohibits a person from acting as an officer of a society if he has been declared unfit to hold office.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: If the amended rules would have the effect of permitting a disqualified person to act as an officer, the Registrar may reject the application.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Ms Ng and Mr Yip asked how this Bill will combat foreign interference through registered societies.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: We already have laws to protect against foreign interference through entities in Singapore, including registered societies and companies.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Once designated, the entity will be subject to countermeasures, such as being required to disclose political donations and foreign affiliations.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: We can also impose additional safeguards on religious groups if there is a greater threat of foreign influence.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Assoc Prof Razwana suggested that "selected societies" be required to provide more details on their governing body at the point of registration.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Dr Syed Harun recognised that the Bill strikes a balance between public safety and interests, while allowing the space for expression in the local communities.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: He also urged MHA to be discerning when making decisions on dissolving societies that have a long track record.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Yip asked about the one-stop service portal for charities.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The intent of the portal is that it would provide a seamless integration between the charities unit and Registry of Societies systems.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Ideally, charities which are also societies will go to one system for their Annual Returns submission.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The details of the one-stop service will be worked out with Charities Unit later.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Yip also asked if groups that are organised in virtual spaces within chat groups and on the Internet will be addressed under the Societies Act and the conditions for their registrations.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: That said, we have to take a practical approach: groups that are transient and informal do not fall under the ambit of the Societies Act.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Giam asked if the amended Automatic Route would deter legitimate groups from registering as a society.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: However, without a legal entity, these groups cannot do things, such as open a bank account in the name of their group or rent a property in the name of their group for their activities.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: And this will likely constrain their ability to attract members.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Assoc Prof Razwana suggested that more resources and information, such as providing mandatory training on rules, countering threats and vulnerabilities, be given to societies which are at higher risks of being exploited by bad actors.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: She also mentioned the formation of online groups on various digital platforms and asked for support to guide them on their compliance obligations.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The relevant domain agencies would provide such information.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: For example, there are available resources for societies to consider, such as the Terrorist Financing Risk Mitigation Toolkit developed by the Charities Unit.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: That said, we will take up Assoc Prof Razwana’s suggestion on how we can provide links to these resources on the ROS website.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: ROS is working on revamping their website and I have asked the team to incorporate Assoc Prof Razwana’s suggestion.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Assoc Prof Razwana also asked MHA to consider introducing explicit whistle-blower protection programmes to encourage and facilitate the reporting of “suspicious” activities.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: At this point, we do not think such measures are necessary.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Individuals can already report “suspicious” activities to the Police and their identities can be protected.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: In particular, under section 127(1) of the Evidence Act, Police officers cannot be compelled to disclose where they got the information from as to the commission of any offence.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Assoc Prof Razwana raised concerns that vulnerable individuals, such as the young, may be susceptible to influence to engage in undesirable or criminal activities when joining a society and asked if there was any support to educate the public.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Such education efforts would be undertaken by the domain agencies rather than the ROS.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: That said, if Assoc Prof Razwana has any specific area of concern, I will bring it back and convey her feedback to the relevant agency.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: For example, $10 will be charged for the online purchase of a society’s constitution.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: We have established work processes between the two Departments and relevant information is exchanged where needed.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: That said, I thank Members for supporting the Bill.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Does this example not show that it is already possible for ROS to change the route of registration without this amendment to the Act?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: The Remaking Singapore Committee chaired by Dr Vivian Balakrishnan proposed this idea in 2003.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Why was it deemed okay then but not now?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: And would the Minister of State agree that this is a reversal of some of the liberalisations introduced in 2004?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: On the second point, indeed, MHA had proposed and created the Automatic Route in 2004.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: That said, we will always have to review the current landscape and look at whether or not the current Act still allows us to stay relevant.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: I, therefore, see the amendments we are proposing today as actually forward-looking.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Any other clarifications for Minister of State Sun?
